questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Identify why governments preferred fixed rates after the 1930s
questions.stem: After the currency collapses of the 1930s, why did most governments choose fixed exchange rates rather than floating ones?

options.text: Fixed rates were adopted because floating had produced beggar-thy-neighbor devaluations and unstable trade.
Gold was abundant enough after 1933 to make every currency convertible on demand.
options.misconception: assumes gold reserves were plentiful rather than scarce

options.text: Floating rates had caused competitive devaluations and trade wars, so fixed parities were meant to restore stability.
options.misconception: confuses the cause of the 1930s collapse with a preference for flexibility

options.text: Governments wanted to eliminate central banks and let markets set all prices.
options.misconception: mistakes a fixed-rate regime for a free-market currency board

questions.explanation: Fixed rates after the 1930s aimed to stop competitive devaluations and restore trade stability. Floating had fueled beggar-thy-neighbor policies, so pegs were chosen for predictability.
questions.hint: Think about what went wrong with floating in the 1930s.

questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the dollar became the reserve currency under a metal peg
questions.stem: Under the postwar fixed-rate system, why did the US dollar become the central reserve currency instead of another national money?

options.text: The dollar was the oldest currency still in circulation, so tradition made it the reserve unit.
The United States held most of the world's gold and ran persistent trade surpluses after 1945.

options.misconception: invents a legal ban that never existed

options.text: The dollar was pegged to silver, which was cheaper and more plentiful than gold.
options.misconception: misidentifies the metal backing the dollar

questions.explanation: US gold dominance and postwar surpluses made the dollar the anchor currency. Other currencies pegged to the dollar, which itself was pegged to gold.
questions.hint: Look at gold holdings and trade balances after 1945.

options.text: The plan that proposed a stabilization fund and a bank for reconstruction.

options.text: Both plans agreed that debtors alone should adjust their economies.
options.misconception: ignores the real disagreement over adjustment burdens

options.text: The plan that proposed a world currency unit and automatic clearing of imbalances.

questions.explanation: The clearing-union plan would have taxed creditor surpluses and eased debtor adjustment. The fund plan instead lent to debtors and kept adjustment on them.

options.misconception: overstates the scope; tariffs were negotiated down gradually

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A decision rule for a club of a hundred
questions.learningObjective: Apply a decision rule that lets a club of many members act
questions.stem: A trading club of a hundred members needs to decide on tariff cuts without letting one member block them. Which voting rule best balances efficiency and legitimacy?

options.text: Unanimity, because every member must consent or the club lacks authority.
options.misconception: ignores the paralysis that unanimity causes in large clubs

options.text: A simple majority, because speed matters more than minority protection.
options.misconception: underestimates the need for broad consent in trade deals

options.text: A qualified majority, requiring a supermajority but not unanimity.
Weighted voting by trade volume, giving large traders an absolute veto.
options.misconception: confuses influence with a blocking power for the largest members

questions.explanation: A qualified majority lets large groups act while protecting minorities from being overridden. Unanimity paralyzes; simple majority risks exclusion; weighted veto empowers giants.
questions.hint: Balance action with protection of minorities.
